subject: Dermatology
q: A 2-week-old neonate develops several flaccid, fragile bullae with clear fluid over the trunk and diaper area, rupturing easily to leave a thin collarette of scale, without surrounding erythema or any systemic illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - localized exfoliative-toxin action confined to the site of bacterial colonization produces flaccid bullae without systemic toxicity
SSSS results from hematogenous spread of the same exfoliative toxin, causing widespread epidermal sloughing, a positive Nikolsky sign, and systemic symptoms
Epidermolysis bullosa is a genetic mechanobullous disorder with blistering from minor trauma or friction present since birth, not an infectious process
Congenital syphilis causes bullae classically on the palms and soles (syphilitic pemphigus) alongside other stigmata, not this diaper-area pattern
exp: Bullous impetigo is caused by exfoliative toxin (ETA/ETB)-producing Staphylococcus aureus acting locally at the site of infection, cleaving desmoglein 1 in the superficial epidermis to produce flaccid, easily ruptured bullae without systemic toxicity - distinct from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, where the same toxin spreads hematogenously to cause widespread sloughing with a positive Nikolsky sign and systemic illness.

subject: Dermatology
q: A young man presents with a slow-growing, mobile, non-tender subcutaneous nodule on the back with a visible central punctum, which occasionally discharges foul-smelling cheesy material. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Lipoma is a soft, lobulated, doughy subcutaneous swelling without a central punctum or discharge
Dermoid cyst is typically a congenital midline or lateral lesion present since birth, without a central punctum
Hidradenitis suppurativa presents with recurrent painful nodules/abscesses and sinus tracts in apocrine areas, not a single mobile nodule with a punctum
Correct - an epidermoid cyst is a slow-growing, mobile subcutaneous nodule with a characteristic central punctum containing keratinous cheesy material
exp: The central punctum is the key clinical clue distinguishing an epidermoid cyst, a keratin-filled cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium arising from a hair follicle infundibulum, from a lipoma or other subcutaneous swelling; definitive treatment is complete surgical excision including the cyst wall to prevent recurrence.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 10-year-old child develops multiple small, drop-like, salmon-pink scaly papules over the trunk and proximal limbs, two weeks after an episode of streptococcal pharyngitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Pityriasis rosea presents with a herald patch followed by smaller lesions in a Christmas-tree distribution after a viral prodrome, not a streptococcal trigger
Nummular eczema presents as coin-shaped, intensely pruritic, often oozing eczematous plaques, unrelated to preceding streptococcal infection
Correct - guttate psoriasis classically presents in children/young adults as small drop-like salmon-pink papules 1-3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis
Pityriasis lichenoides presents with recurrent crops of papules that can be hemorrhagic/necrotic, without this specific post-streptococcal trigger
exp: Guttate psoriasis is a distinct, often self-limited variant of psoriasis triggered by streptococcal infection, thought to involve molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and keratinocyte antigens, presenting with numerous small raindrop lesions; it can resolve spontaneously or evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis in some patients.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 14-year-old presents with multiple small dark brown to black macules around the lips, buccal mucosa, and fingertips, along with recurrent episodes of colicky abdominal pain. Family history reveals similar pigmentation in the mother. What underlying condition should be suspected?
why: McCune-Albright syndrome features irregular coast-of-Maine café-au-lait macules, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and precocious puberty, not perioral mucosal pigmentation
Correct - Peutz-Jeghers syndrome presents with mucocutaneous melanotic macules on the lips, buccal mucosa, and digits, along with hamartomatous GI polyps, often with a family history
Neurofibromatosis type 1 features smooth coast-of-California café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules, not this perioral pattern
Addison disease causes diffuse hyperpigmentation with additional features of adrenal insufficiency, not localized perioral macules with GI polyps
exp: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome's mucocutaneous pigmented macules are present from infancy/childhood and often fade with age on the skin but persist on mucosa, serving as an external clue to underlying hamartomatous GI polyposis, which carries an increased lifetime risk of both GI and extra-GI malignancy requiring surveillance.

subject: Dermatology
q: A patient with a painless genital ulcer has a reactive VDRL test. To confirm the diagnosis of syphilis and rule out a biological false-positive VDRL (as can occur in conditions like SLE or antiphospholipid syndrome), which test should be performed next?
why: Correct - TPHA is a treponeme-specific test that confirms true syphilis infection and remains positive for life, distinguishing it from a biological false-positive VDRL
Repeating VDRL after treatment is used to monitor treatment response, not to confirm the initial diagnosis
Dark-field microscopy of ulcer exudate can demonstrate spirochetes directly but requires an active moist lesion and immediate specialized microscopy, not the standard next step here
Tzanck smear detects multinucleated giant cells in herpesvirus infections, unrelated to syphilis diagnosis
exp: VDRL/RPR are non-treponemal tests that are excellent for screening but can give biological false positives in autoimmune disease, pregnancy, and other infections; a treponemal test such as TPHA or FTA-ABS is required for confirmation, and unlike VDRL titers, treponemal tests typically remain positive for life even after successful treatment, so they cannot be used to monitor treatment response.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 34-year-old woman with a 6-year history of ulcerative colitis presents with a rapidly enlarging, painful leg ulcer that started as a small pustule. Examination shows a violaceous, undermined border with a necrotic base, and minor trauma to nearby normal skin produced a similar new lesion. What is the diagnosis?
why: Correct - violaceous undermined border plus pathergy plus IBD association is classic.
Necrotizing fasciitis is acutely septic, rapidly spreading with severe pain/crepitus/systemic toxicity, not a chronic undermined ulcer.
Venous ulcers occur over the medial malleolus with hemosiderin/lipodermatosclerosis, not undermined violaceous borders or pathergy.
Lupus vulgaris is a slowly progressive apple-jelly nodular plaque, not an acute pathergic ulcer.
exp: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis strongly associated with IBD (UC more than Crohn's), RA, and myeloproliferative disease. It shows pathergy (new lesions at trauma sites); treatment is systemic immunosuppression and surgical debridement can worsen it - a classic exam trap.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 45-year-old man presents with tense, itchy bullae over the trunk and limbs. To confirm the suspected diagnosis by direct immunofluorescence, a skin biopsy is planned. From where should the biopsy be taken for the DIF sample to be most reliable?
opts: Any lesional skin, site does not matter
Perilesional normal-appearing skin adjacent to a lesion
why: A fresh intact bulla is preferred for routine H&E, not the standard DIF site.
A de-roofed/ulcerated base has lost epidermis and immunoreactants, giving false-negative DIF.
Random lesional skin risks false-negative DIF from degraded immunoreactants.
Correct - perilesional normal skin best preserves the immune deposits for DIF.
exp: For direct immunofluorescence in immunobullous disease (pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis), biopsy must be taken from perilesional, clinically normal-appearing skin within about 1 cm of a lesion, because immune deposits are best preserved there while lesional skin often shows degraded immunoreactants.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 27-year-old man presents 3 weeks after an episode of urethral discharge with asymmetric oligoarthritis of the knee and ankle, conjunctivitis, and painless, shallow, circinate erosions on the glans penis. A urethral swab at the time had shown Chlamydia trachomatis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - classic post-chlamydial reactive arthritis triad.
Secondary syphilis causes palmoplantar rash and condylomata lata with positive serology, not this triad.
Behcet causes oral/genital ulcers and uveitis but lacks this post-urethritis temporal link and circinate balanitis pattern.
Disseminated gonococcal infection shows tenosynovitis/pustules with culture-positive live organisms, not a sterile post-infectious reaction.
exp: Reactive arthritis is a post-infectious seronegative spondyloarthropathy triggered by genitourinary (Chlamydia trachomatis) or enteric infection, presenting 1-4 weeks later with asymmetric oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis, and circinate balanitis/keratoderma blennorrhagicum. It is HLA-B27 associated, and cultures are sterile.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 6-year-old boy is brought with multiple flat, uniformly light-brown patches on the trunk, the largest measuring 2 cm, along with freckling in both axillae. His father has similar skin findings and multiple soft skin-colored nodules. Which finding would confirm the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Wood's lamp showing enhanced contrast of the patches
KOH mount showing hyphae from a patch
Six or more cafe-au-lait macules each greater than 5 mm in this prepubertal child
Skin biopsy showing loss of melanocytes
why: Wood's lamp enhances hypopigmented lesions such as vitiligo, not hyperpigmented macules already visible in normal light.
KOH/hyphae would suggest tinea, irrelevant to uniformly pigmented flat macules with this family pattern.
Correct - satisfies the NIH diagnostic criterion for NF1.
Biopsy showing melanocyte loss describes vitiligo, not a hyperpigmented macule.
exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically (classic NIH criteria; a revised 2021 scheme also exists): six or more cafe-au-lait macules (over 5 mm prepubertal, over 15 mm postpubertal) plus axillary/inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic glioma, a distinctive osseous lesion, or an affected first-degree relative; two criteria confirm the diagnosis.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 19-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding and pica (craving for ice) presents with fatigue and brittle nails that have become thin, flattened, and spoon-shaped with everted edges that can hold a drop of water. What is the most likely underlying cause of this nail change?
why: Psoriasis produces nail pitting and the oil-drop sign, not spoon-shaped concavity.
Onychomycosis causes thickened, discolored, dystrophic nails with subungual debris, not a smooth spoon shape.
Cyanosis affects nail bed color, not nail plate shape.
Correct - classic iron-deficiency nail sign.
exp: Koilonychia (spoon-shaped, concave nails with everted edges) is classically associated with chronic iron deficiency anemia, also seen in Plummer-Vinson syndrome and hemochromatosis. Correcting the anemia typically reverses the nail change over months.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 13-year-old obese boy is brought with dark, velvety, thickened skin over the nape of the neck and axillae, noticed gradually over the past year; he has no history of weight loss or systemic illness.
why: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation follows a preceding inflammatory dermatosis or trauma at that site, not symmetric velvety thickening
Addison's disease causes diffuse bronze hyperpigmentation with systemic features like fatigue and hypotension, not localized flexural change
Tinea versicolor shows hypo or hyperpigmented scaly macules with a spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern on KOH, not velvety thickening
Correct: acanthosis nigricans in an obese adolescent is a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance
exp: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese adolescent without weight loss is a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance from obesity, PCOS, or type 2 diabetes rather than internal malignancy, which is the concern in older, non-obese, rapid-onset cases, and warrants screening for dysglycemia and metabolic syndrome.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 28-year-old woman develops an itchy, erythematous, well-demarcated rash exactly at the site of contact with a metal belt buckle and cheap earrings, resolving on avoidance; suspected allergic contact dermatitis to nickel. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the causative allergen?
opts: Patch test with delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reading at 48-96 hours
Prick test with immediate reading at 15-20 minutes
why: Correct: patch testing confirms a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity like nickel allergic contact dermatitis, read at 48 and 96 hours
Prick test with immediate reading detects IgE-mediated type I allergy such as food or aeroallergen sensitization, not contact dermatitis
Direct immunofluorescence diagnoses immunobullous or connective tissue disease, not allergen identification
KOH mount detects fungal elements, irrelevant to allergic contact dermatitis workup
exp: Allergic contact dermatitis, such as to nickel in jewelry or buckles, is a type IV delayed T-cell mediated hypersensitivity reaction; patch testing applies the suspected allergen under occlusion and is read at 48 and 96 hours, unlike prick testing used for type I immediate allergies.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 6-week-old infant presents with a persistent nasal discharge (snuffles), hepatosplenomegaly, and a maculopapular rash on the palms and soles; the mother had untreated syphilis during pregnancy and delayed antenatal care.
why: Congenital rubella causes cataract, patent ductus arteriosus, and sensorineural deafness classically, not snuffles or palmoplantar rash
Correct: early congenital syphilis presents with persistent rhinitis, hepatosplenomegaly, and palmoplantar maculopapular rash
Neonatal HSV causes vesicular skin lesions, encephalitis, or disseminated disease, not classic snuffles
Congenital toxoplasmosis causes the classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications, not this presentation
exp: Early congenital syphilis, presenting before 2 years of age, shows persistent rhinitis or snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, palmoplantar maculopapular or desquamative rash, and osteochondritis; late congenital syphilis if untreated manifests later with Hutchinson's triad of interstitial keratitis, Hutchinson teeth, and 8th nerve deafness, and is treated with penicillin.

subject: Dermatology
q: A dermatologist evaluating a patient before laser hair removal notes the patient's skin always burns and never tans on sun exposure, with fair skin and red hair, and classifies the risk of post-procedure pigmentary change accordingly.
why: Type IV tans well with minimal burning, typical of Indian or Mediterranean skin, carrying higher pigmentary risk with lasers
Type V rarely burns and tans darkly, typical of brown skin
Correct: type I skin always burns and never tans, carrying the highest sunburn risk but lowest laser-induced pigmentation risk
Type VI never burns, is deeply pigmented, and carries the highest dyspigmentation risk with lasers
exp: The Fitzpatrick skin phototype classification grades skin from I to VI based on burning versus tanning tendency; type I, fair skin often with red hair, always burns and never tans, carrying the highest sunburn and photodamage risk but the lowest risk of laser-induced post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation compared with darker types.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 45-year-old fair-skinned woman presents with recurrent facial flushing, persistent erythema, and papulopustules over the central face (cheeks, nose, chin) for several months, worsened by sun exposure, spicy food, and alcohol, without comedones.
why: Acne vulgaris characteristically shows open or closed comedones, which are absent here
Seborrheic dermatitis shows greasy yellowish scaling in the nasolabial folds, eyebrows, and scalp, not papulopustules
Perioral dermatitis is typically linked to topical steroid use and localized strictly around the mouth sparing a vermilion rim
Correct: rosacea is a chronic sebaceous and vascular disorder of the central face with flushing, erythema, and papulopustules without comedones
exp: Rosacea is a chronic disorder of the central face with flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, and papulopustules without comedones, triggered by heat, alcohol, spicy food, and sun exposure, managed with trigger avoidance, topical metronidazole or azelaic acid, and oral doxycycline for moderate to severe disease.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 45-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic, violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped papules over the flexor aspects of both wrists, along with white lacy streaks on the buccal mucosa. Which best describes the characteristic histopathological finding in this condition?
opts: Subepidermal bulla with an eosinophil-rich infiltrate
Granular IgA deposits at dermal papillary tips
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction with saw-tooth rete ridges
Intraepidermal acantholysis with a row of tombstones basal layer
why: This describes bullous pemphigoid histology, not lichen planus
This describes dermatitis herpetiformis, not lichen planus
Correct - lichen planus shows a lichenoid, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate with saw-toothed rete ridges
This describes pemphigus vulgaris (acantholysis, tombstone basal cells), not lichen planus
exp: Lichen planus (the 6 P's: pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules, plaques) with Wickham striae on mucosa shows a lichenoid band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction; consider hepatitis C screening in these patients.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless, beefy-red genital ulcer with rolled edges that bleeds easily on touch, present for 3 weeks, without significant regional lymphadenopathy. Giemsa staining of a tissue smear shows intracytoplasmic safety-pin shaped organisms within macrophages. Which organism is responsible?
why: Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful ragged ulcer with tender suppurative lymphadenopathy, not painless beefy-red
Correct - Klebsiella granulomatis causes donovanosis, with Donovan bodies on Giemsa stain and no true lymphadenopathy
Treponema pallidum causes the painless indurated chancre of primary syphilis, without the friable beefy-red character described
Chlamydia L1-L3 causes lymphogranuloma venereum, with prominent painful buboes, not this ulcer morphology
exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale), from Klebsiella granulomatis, gives a painless, beefy-red, friable ulcer with Donovan bodies on Giemsa/Wright stain and characteristically no true regional lymphadenopathy (pseudobuboes may form instead).

subject: Dermatology
q: A 58-year-old man with longstanding, poorly-controlled type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with rapidly spreading erythema and edema over the leg, hemorrhagic bullae, and pain markedly out of proportion to the visible skin findings, with crepitus on palpation. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Urgent surgical debridement along with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Intravenous antibiotics alone with close monitoring
Incision and drainage under local anesthesia in the outpatient department
Topical silver sulfadiazine dressing and elevation
why: Correct - necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency requiring prompt debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics
Antibiotics alone without debridement fail to achieve source control and worsen mortality
Outpatient management is grossly inadequate for a life-threatening, rapidly progressive infection
Topical dressing has no role in an emergency requiring surgical source control
exp: Pain out of proportion to exam findings, crepitus, rapidly spreading erythema, and hemorrhagic bullae in a diabetic patient are red flags for necrotizing fasciitis, which needs early aggressive surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics - delay increases mortality.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman develops symmetric, hyperpigmented brown patches over the malar cheeks, forehead, and upper lip that darken with sun exposure. Wood's lamp examination shows accentuation of the pigmentation. Which type of melasma does this finding suggest, and what is its clinical significance?
opts: Dermal type - pigment is in the papillary/reticular dermis and responds poorly to topical bleaching agents
Mixed type - equal contribution from epidermis and dermis, unaffected by Wood's lamp
Wood's lamp accentuation indicates this is not melasma but post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
Epidermal type - pigment is confined to the epidermis and responds better to topical bleaching agents
why: Dermal type shows no accentuation under Wood's lamp, contrary to this finding
Mixed type shows only partial accentuation, not equal and unaffected
The picture (symmetric malar pigmentation in pregnancy) is classic melasma, not post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation which follows a preceding inflammatory lesion
Correct - epidermal melasma accentuates under Wood's lamp and responds better to topical bleaching agents such as hydroquinone
exp: On Wood's lamp, epidermal melasma shows accentuated pigment contrast because pigment lies near the surface, and this type responds better to topical depigmenting therapy than dermal melasma, where pigment (melanophages) lies deeper and Wood's lamp shows no accentuation.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 22-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, non-pitting swelling of the face and hands along with episodes of severe abdominal pain, lasting 2-3 days each, since adolescence. There is no associated urticaria, and antihistamines have not helped. Her father had similar episodes. Which is the most likely underlying deficiency?
why: C3 deficiency predisposes to recurrent pyogenic infections, not angioedema
Mast cell tryptase excess suggests mastocytosis, typically with urticaria pigmentosa and flushing
Correct - hereditary angioedema results from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, causing unregulated bradykinin-driven angioedema unresponsive to antihistamines
IgE-mediated angioedema is typically associated with urticaria and responds to antihistamines, unlike this case
exp: Hereditary angioedema (autosomal dominant, C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency) causes recurrent non-pruritic, non-urticarial swelling and painful abdominal attacks from bowel wall edema, and does not respond to antihistamines, steroids, or epinephrine.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 9-year-old girl, going through a stressful school transition, is brought with an irregular patch of hair loss on the scalp with hairs of varying lengths, some broken close to the scalp, but no scaling, erythema, or exclamation-mark hairs, and a normal hair pull test at the margins. Which diagnosis is most likely, and how does it differ from alopecia areata?
opts: Alopecia areata; smooth, well-demarcated patch with exclamation-mark hairs at the margin
Tinea capitis; expect scaling and positive KOH mount
Telogen effluvium; expect diffuse rather than patchy hair loss
Trichotillomania; irregular patch with hairs of differing lengths from repeated hair-pulling, not a smooth bald patch
why: Describes classic alopecia areata, not this case.
Tinea capitis would show scaling/broken stubs with a positive KOH, not mentioned here.
Telogen effluvium is diffuse scalp-wide shedding, not a localized patch.
Correct - repetitive hair-pulling produces an irregular patch with variable hair lengths and an intact, non-scarred scalp.
exp: Trichotillomania (often stress-triggered) is distinguished from alopecia areata by an irregular border and hairs broken at varying lengths, versus alopecia areata's smooth, completely bald patch with tapering exclamation-mark hairs and a positive pull test at the active margin.

subject: Dermatology
q: Three weeks after starting phenytoin for a seizure disorder, a 14-year-old develops a widespread morbilliform rash, facial edema, fever, and marked eosinophilia and deranged liver enzymes on blood work. Which drug reaction is most likely, and what distinguishes it from a simple morbilliform drug rash?
opts: DRESS syndrome; delayed onset (2-8 weeks), eosinophilia, and internal organ (commonly hepatic) involvement
Fixed drug eruption; recurs at the same site on re-exposure
Urticaria; resolves within 24 hours of antihistamine use
Serum sickness; mediated by immune complex deposition without eosinophilia
why: Correct - DRESS is a delayed (2-8 week), severe hypersensitivity reaction with fever, facial edema, eosinophilia, and organ involvement, classically triggered by aromatic anticonvulsants.
Fixed drug eruption recurs at a fixed site, not as a systemic eosinophilic reaction.
Simple urticaria does not cause fever, eosinophilia, or organ involvement.
Serum sickness is immune-complex mediated with arthralgia/urticaria, not typically this latency/eosinophilia pattern.
exp: DRESS syndrome carries significant mortality if unrecognized and demands immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, sulfonamides, allopurinol are classic triggers) - the 2-8 week latency and organ involvement (usually hepatic) are the key differentiators from an ordinary morbilliform rash.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 16-year-old with longstanding unexplained iron-deficiency anemia and intermittent loose stools develops intensely itchy, grouped vesicles symmetrically over the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillary tips. What underlying systemic condition should be evaluated for?
why: Not the classic systemic association of this rash.
Correct - dermatitis herpetiformis is the cutaneous manifestation of gluten sensitivity, almost always associated with celiac disease.
IBD is not the recognized association of dermatitis herpetiformis.
Hepatitis B has no established link to this rash.
exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (grouped, intensely itchy vesicles over extensor surfaces, granular IgA at the dermal papillary tips) should always prompt screening for celiac disease, even when GI symptoms are subtle - both rash and malabsorption typically respond to a strict gluten-free diet.

subject: Dermatology
q: On examining a patient with a blistering skin eruption, a resident needs to correctly classify the primary lesion in the case notes. Using the standard dermatological size convention, a fluid-filled lesion measuring 1.2 cm in diameter would be correctly termed:
opts: A vesicle, because it is fluid-filled and raised
A pustule, since any raised fluid-filled lesion over 1 cm is a pustule
A bulla, since fluid-filled lesions greater than 0.5-1 cm are termed bullae rather than vesicles
A wheal, because of its size
why: Describes a vesicle, but the size here exceeds the vesicle cutoff.
A pustule is defined by purulent (not clear) fluid content, not size.
Correct - a bulla is a fluid-filled lesion larger than the ~0.5-1 cm vesicle cutoff.
A wheal is a transient, edematous, non-fluid-filled papule/plaque, unrelated to blister size.
exp: Correctly naming primary lesions (macule/papule, vesicle/bulla, pustule, wheal) by strict size and content criteria is the first step to building a dermatology differential - a 1.2 cm clear blister is a bulla, not a vesicle.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 5-year-old presents with multiple small, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured papules with a characteristic central dimple (umbilication), scattered over the trunk and axilla, mildly itchy but not painful. What is the most likely diagnosis and causative organism?
opts: Verruca vulgaris caused by human papillomavirus
Milia caused by trapped keratin, non-infectious
Molluscum contagiosum caused by a poxvirus
why: Verruca (warts) are rough, hyperkeratotic papules without central umbilication.
Milia are tiny superficial keratin cysts without umbilication, non-infectious.
Varicella presents as pruritic vesicles on an erythematous base in crops, not umbilicated papules.
Correct - molluscum contagiosum, caused by a DNA poxvirus, produces dome-shaped, pearly, umbilicated papules.
exp: Molluscum contagiosum spreads by direct skin contact or fomites and is usually self-limited over months in an immunocompetent child, but can be more extensive or persistent in atopic or immunocompromised children.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 34-year-old man with plaque psoriasis develops yellowish oil-drop discoloration and distal onycholysis of his fingernails. Which additional nail finding is most specific for psoriatic nail disease rather than dermatophyte onychomycosis?
opts: Coarse, irregular ('geometric') pitting of the nail plate, reflecting nail-matrix involvement
Subungual hyperkeratosis with a crumbling, friable nail plate
Yellow-white longitudinal streaks (dermatophytoma) within the nail plate
Distal-lateral subungual onycholysis with green-black discoloration (Pseudomonas colonization)
why: Correct -- nail-matrix pitting, essentially absent in onychomycosis, is the other specific psoriasis discriminator alongside the oil-drop sign.
Crumbling nail with subungual hyperkeratosis leans toward onychomycosis, not psoriasis.
Dermatophytoma streaks are a fungal-ball finding characteristic of onychomycosis.
Green-black discoloration signals secondary Pseudomonas colonization of an onycholytic nail, not psoriasis.
exp: Nail-matrix pitting is a psoriasis-specific finding essentially absent in onychomycosis (a nail-bed/plate process); together with the oil-drop sign, it is the strongest bedside discriminator from fungal onychomycosis.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 26-year-old woman develops a solitary, sharply demarcated, dusky violaceous plaque on the lip within hours of taking co-trimoxazole for a UTI, with residual hyperpigmentation from an identical episode at the same site during a previous course of the same drug.
why: EM minor is HSV-triggered with multi-site target lesions, not a recurring solitary fixed-site plaque.
Recurrence of an identical lesion at the same site with drug re-exposure, leaving residual hyperpigmentation, is pathognomonic for fixed drug eruption.
Bullous pemphigoid occurs in the elderly with tense bullae, unrelated to drug timing at a fixed site.
Contact dermatitis follows topical allergen exposure, not oral drug intake, and does not recur with systemic drug re-exposure.
exp: Fixed drug eruption recurs at the identical cutaneous or mucosal site with each re-exposure to the culprit drug and leaves residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; co-trimoxazole is one of the classic triggers to know for exams.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 45-year-old man presents with flaccid, easily ruptured bullae over the trunk and oral erosions. A Tzanck smear from the base of a fresh blister shows rounded, detached keratinocytes with hyperchromatic nuclei and loss of intercellular bridges.
opts: Multinucleated giant cells with nuclear molding
why: Multinucleated giant cells with molding are the Tzanck-smear finding in herpes simplex/VZV infection, not this presentation.
Dutcher bodies are intranuclear pseudo-inclusions of lymphoplasmacytic disorders, unrelated to skin cytology.
Rounded, detached keratinocytes with hyperchromatic nuclei and loss of intercellular bridges are acantholytic cells, diagnostic of pemphigus vulgaris.
Civatte bodies are apoptotic keratinocytes seen on lichen planus histopathology, not on a Tzanck smear.
exp: Acantholytic (Tzanck) cells on a smear from a fresh bullous lesion are the bedside cytological clue to pemphigus vulgaris, distinct from the multinucleated giant cells with molding seen in herpetic infections.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 9-year-old girl presents with fatigue, salt craving, and hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, gingiva, and palmar creases, more pronounced than in sun-exposed skin. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?
opts: Increased melanocyte density from chronic UV exposure
Elevated ACTH/POMC-derived peptides cross-stimulating melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes
why: UV-driven pigmentation would spare mucosa and palmar creases and would not explain the systemic symptoms.
Dermal iron deposition causes a slate-grey pigmentation pattern, not this mucosal/crease-predominant one.
Post-inflammatory pigmentation follows a preceding inflammatory dermatosis at that specific site, not this diffuse pattern.
In primary adrenal insufficiency, loss of cortisol feedback raises ACTH/POMC, whose melanocyte-stimulating fragments activate MC1R, producing this pigmentation pattern.
exp: Mucosal, gingival, and palmar-crease hyperpigmentation with fatigue and salt craving in a child points to primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease); the pigmentation arises because elevated ACTH/POMC-derived peptides cross-stimulate melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 28-year-old woman treated with topical clobetasol for presumed eczema on the leg develops follicular, boggy, pustular nodules despite treatment. KOH mount from a nodule shows fungal hyphae invading hair follicles.
why: Topical corticosteroid use over unrecognised dermatophyte infection, with fungal invasion extending into the hair follicle producing boggy follicular nodules, defines Majocchi granuloma.
Tinea incognito is the broader umbrella term for any steroid-modified atypical tinea, without specifically implying follicular invasion on KOH.
Folliculitis decalvans is a non-fungal, neutrophilic scarring alopecia.
Kerion is an inflammatory, boggy tinea capitis reaction typically on the scalp in children, not the leg in an adult.
exp: Majocchi granuloma is follicular/perifollicular dermatophyte invasion that develops when topical corticosteroids are used on unrecognised tinea, classically on the legs of women after shaving; KOH shows hyphae invading the follicle itself, distinguishing it from simple steroid-modified tinea (tinea incognito).

subject: Dermatology
q: A 30-year-old farmer presents with a single hypopigmented, well-defined, anaesthetic patch over the left forearm. The ulnar nerve is not thickened. Slit-skin smear shows no acid-fast bacilli, and a skin biopsy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with few lymphocytes at the periphery. Which type of leprosy does this represent?
why: Lepromatous leprosy shows numerous symmetric lesions with abundant bacilli (multibacillary) — wrong pole of the spectrum for this single paucibacillary lesion.
Borderline lepromatous also carries a higher bacillary load and more numerous lesions than described.
Correct — single anaesthetic patch, negative smear, well-formed granuloma = tuberculoid, the paucibacillary, high cell-mediated-immunity end.
Indeterminate leprosy is the earliest, non-specific stage with a vague hypopigmented patch and no clear granuloma formation on biopsy — this case already shows well-formed granulomas.
exp: Tuberculoid leprosy sits at the high-immunity pole of the Ridley-Jopling spectrum: single/few well-defined, anaesthetic, hypopigmented patches, strong granulomatous response, paucibacillary (negative slit-skin smear) — contrast with lepromatous leprosy at the low-immunity pole (multiple, ill-defined, symmetric, bacilli-laden lesions).

subject: Dermatology
q: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with yellow, thickened, and crumbly toenails of several months' duration. A KOH mount of nail clippings shows septate, branching hyphae. What is the most appropriate first-line oral treatment?
why: Fluconazole is reserved for Candida-predominant onychomycosis, not the first choice for dermatophyte infection.
Correct — terbinafine has the best cure rates and nail penetration for dermatophyte onychomycosis.
Itraconazole pulse therapy is an effective alternative but not the first-line choice over terbinafine.
Griseofulvin has largely been abandoned for onychomycosis due to prolonged courses and lower cure rates.
exp: Dermatophyte onychomycosis (tinea unguium) is confirmed by septate hyphae on KOH. Oral terbinafine is first-line because of its high nail-keratin affinity and superior mycological cure rates versus azoles — typically 6 weeks for fingernails, 12 weeks for toenails.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 60-year-old man on long-standing phenytoin develops progressive, diffuse erythema and fine scaling involving more than 90% of his body surface area, with associated shivering, lymphadenopathy, and hypoalbuminemia. What is this presentation called?
why: Correct — diffuse confluent erythema/scaling over ≥90% BSA with systemic derangement is the definition of erythroderma.
TEN presents with mucocutaneous blistering and epidermal detachment (Nikolsky-positive), not simple diffuse scaling erythema.
Pemphigus foliaceus produces superficial crusted erosions, not a diffusely scaly erythrodermic picture.
Generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch) shows sheets of sterile pustules on erythematous skin, which is not described here.
exp: Erythroderma is diffuse erythema/scaling over ≥90% BSA; drugs (phenytoin, sulfonamides), pre-existing dermatoses, and lymphoma are classic causes. It carries systemic risk — hypothermia, high-output cardiac failure, protein/fluid loss, secondary sepsis — needing inpatient supportive care.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 22-year-old woman presents with well-demarcated, milky-white, non-scaly macules over the hands and around the mouth, present for 6 months. Under Wood's lamp examination in a dark room, the lesions show enhanced chalky-white fluorescence. Screening for which associated condition is most appropriate?
why: Iron deficiency is not a recognized autoimmune comorbidity of vitiligo.
CKD has no established autoimmune association with vitiligo.
Asthma is not part of the classic autoimmune cluster linked to vitiligo.
Correct — vitiligo is strongly associated with autoimmune thyroid disease, and thyroid screening is standard in newly diagnosed patients.
exp: Vitiligo results from autoimmune melanocyte destruction and shows enhanced chalky-white fluorescence under Wood's lamp (365nm), helping delineate borders/subclinical lesions in fair skin. It clusters with other autoimmune disease, most commonly autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis — TSH/anti-TPO screening is routine.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 24-year-old sexually active man presents with a cluster of painful, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the glans penis, with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. A Tzanck smear from a de-roofed vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: A syphilitic chancre is a single, painless, indurated ulcer, not a cluster of painful vesicles.
Correct — painful grouped vesicles plus a positive Tzanck smear for multinucleated giant cells is classic for HSV.
LGV presents with a transient painless papule/ulcer followed by painful matted inguinal buboes weeks later, not vesicles.
Molluscum contagiosum causes umbilicated, painless papules, not painful vesicles, and would not show multinucleated giant cells.
exp: Genital herpes classically presents as grouped, painful vesicles on an erythematous base eroding into shallow ulcers, with tender regional lymphadenopathy. A Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells supports herpesvirus infection, though HSV PCR/culture is confirmatory; first episodes are often more severe than recurrences.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a sharply demarcated, raised, fiery-red, warm, tender plaque over the left cheek with an advancing indurated border, associated with fever and chills. What is the most likely diagnosis and its usual causative organism?
opts: Necrotizing fasciitis due to polymicrobial flora
Erysipelas due to group A Streptococcus
why: Cellulitis (usually S. aureus or Streptococcus) involves deeper dermis/subcutis and has poorly defined, non-raised borders, unlike this sharply marginated plaque.
Necrotizing fasciitis presents with rapidly progressive pain out of proportion, skin necrosis, and systemic toxicity, not a well-demarcated erythematous plaque.
Correct — a sharply demarcated, raised, fiery-red plaque is the hallmark of erysipelas, classically streptococcal.
Impetigo is a superficial infection with honey-colored crusted lesions, not a deep tender erythematous plaque.
exp: Erysipelas is a superficial dermal infection, classically caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, presenting with a sharply demarcated, raised, fiery-red plaque with a clear advancing border — the sharp demarcation is the key clue distinguishing it from cellulitis, which involves deeper tissue with poorly defined margins.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 19-year-old woman has moderate inflammatory acne with papules, pustules, a few nodules, and comedones over the face and back, unresponsive to 3 months of topical benzoyl peroxide combined with topical clindamycin. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Add a topical retinoid alone and stop other agents
Add an oral antibiotic such as doxycycline while continuing topical therapy
why: Isotretinoin is not first-line without a prior oral antibiotic trial or evidence of scarring/severe nodulocystic disease
Retinoid alone fails to address the inflammatory/bacterial component needed for escalation
Correct - oral antibiotic combined with continued topical therapy is the next step for moderate acne unresponsive to topicals
Oral corticosteroids have no role in routine acne management
exp: The acne treatment ladder escalates from topical therapy to an oral antibiotic (doxycycline or a macrolide) combined with continued topical treatment for moderate inflammatory acne unresponsive to topicals alone; oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulocystic acne, scarring, or failure of oral antibiotic combination therapy.

subject: Dermatology
q: A young man notices multiple soft, papillary, cauliflower-like growths on the glans penis, painless and non-indurated, with no regional lymphadenopathy. Histopathology shows koilocytes. Which condition does this most likely represent?
why: Condylomata lata are flat, moist, broad-based plaques showing spirochetes, not koilocytes.
Correct - condylomata acuminata are HPV-induced papillary warts with characteristic koilocytes on histopathology.
Molluscum contagiosum shows umbilicated papules with Henderson-Patterson bodies, not koilocytes.
Donovanosis shows beefy-red ulcers with Donovan bodies, not papillary warts.
exp: Condylomata acuminata are HPV (commonly types 6 and 11)-induced genital warts presenting as soft, papillary, cauliflower-like, painless growths; koilocytes (perinuclear halo with nuclear atypia) on histopathology are the classic diagnostic feature.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 30-year-old woman reports diffuse hair thinning and increased shedding noticed on her pillow and in the shower, beginning about 3 months after a severe febrile illness and significant weight loss, with no scalp scarring or patchy bald areas on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Alopecia areata presents with well-demarcated patchy bald areas and exclamation-mark hairs, not diffuse shedding
Correct - diffuse shedding 2-3 months after a stressor defines telogen effluvium
Androgenetic alopecia is a gradual, patterned thinning tied to androgen sensitivity, not an acute post-stressor event
Tinea capitis presents with scaly patches and broken hairs, not simple diffuse shedding
exp: Telogen effluvium is diffuse, non-scarring hair shedding occurring 2-3 months after a triggering stressor, due to a premature shift of anagen hairs into telogen phase - typically self-limiting, resolving within 6 months.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 26-year-old man presents with gradual, progressive hair thinning over the bitemporal regions and vertex over the past 3 years, with a family history of similar pattern baldness in his father and maternal grandfather, and no scalp scaling, itching, or patchy loss on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis and its typical classification system?
opts: Androgenetic alopecia, classified by Norwood-Hamilton scale
Alopecia areata, classified by SALT score
Telogen effluvium, classified by Ludwig scale
Tinea capitis, classified by Trichoscopy score
why: Correct - bitemporal-vertex pattern with family history and Norwood-Hamilton grading
Alopecia areata is patchy and autoimmune, and the SALT score quantifies scalp area affected, not this pattern
Telogen effluvium is diffuse and acute, and the Ludwig scale is used for female pattern hair loss
Tinea capitis is an infectious cause with scaling, not seen here
exp: Androgenetic alopecia (male pattern hair loss) is a genetically determined, androgen-mediated progressive miniaturization of hair follicles in a bitemporal-to-vertex pattern, classified using the Norwood-Hamilton scale.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 16-year-old girl develops a single oval, scaly, salmon-colored patch on her trunk. One week later, several smaller similar lesions appear along the skin cleavage lines of her back, forming a pattern resembling a Christmas tree, with mild associated itching. What is the most likely diagnosis and expected course?
opts: Guttate psoriasis, requiring long-term topical steroids
why: Guttate psoriasis shows well-demarcated silvery scaly papules, usually post-streptococcal, without a herald patch
Secondary syphilis causes a papulosquamous rash typically involving palms/soles with positive serology, not a herald-patch progression
Tinea corporis shows an annular lesion with active border and central clearing, KOH-positive
Correct — classic herald patch followed by the Christmas-tree pattern
exp: Pityriasis rosea is a self-limiting papulosquamous eruption (probably HHV-6/7 related) beginning with a single herald patch followed within days to weeks by smaller oval lesions distributed along skin cleavage lines (Langer's lines) on the trunk, giving the classic Christmas-tree pattern on the back; reassurance is the mainstay since it resolves spontaneously in 6-8 weeks.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 32-year-old man presents with painful, matted inguinal lymphadenopathy above and below the inguinal ligament producing a 'groove sign,' two weeks after a small painless genital ulcer that healed spontaneously unnoticed. What is the most likely causative organism?
why: H. ducreyi (chancroid) causes painful ulcers with painful suppurative unilateral lymphadenopathy, not the groove sign
T. pallidum causes a painless chancre with generalized lymphadenopathy
Correct — LGV from C. trachomatis L1-L3 produces the pathognomonic groove sign
Klebsiella granulomatis causes granuloma inguinale with beefy-red ulceration and pseudobuboes, not true lymphadenopathy
exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3, classically has three stages — a transient painless ulcer, followed weeks later by painful inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy that can straddle the inguinal ligament producing the pathognomonic 'groove sign,' and a late anogenitorectal syndrome if untreated.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 35-year-old man has well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales over extensor knees and elbows; scraping produces pinpoint bleeding, and new plaques appear along a recent scratch mark. What are these two signs called respectively?
why: Nikolsky sign is a pemphigus/TEN finding, not the pinpoint-bleeding sign
Darier sign (urtication on stroking) is seen in mastocytosis
Correct — Auspitz sign and Koebner phenomenon are classic psoriasis signs
Dennie-Morgan fold is an atopic dermatitis finding
exp: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removing psoriatic scale, due to thinned suprapapillary epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries) and the Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon (new lesions at trauma sites) are two classic bedside signs supporting a clinical diagnosis of psoriasis.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 6-year-old boy presents with multiple superficial erosions on the face covered by golden-yellow, honey-colored crusts, developing at the site of a minor insect bite. The lesions are mildly itchy but non-tender, and he is afebrile. What is the most likely diagnosis and its most common causative organism?
opts: Non-bullous impetigo, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus
why: Correct — honey-colored crusted erosions are classic non-bullous impetigo, usually S. aureus
Erysipelas is a deeper, sharply demarcated, tender plaque with systemic symptoms, not a superficial crusted erosion
Cellulitis presents as diffuse, tender, warm skin/subcutaneous infection, often with fever
Ecthyma is a deeper ulcerative form leaving a punched-out ulcer; Pseudomonas is not its typical cause
exp: Non-bullous impetigo (the most common form) presents as superficial erosions with a characteristic golden-yellow ('honey-colored') crust, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus (with Streptococcus pyogenes also implicated in some cases) — topical mupirocin is first-line for localized disease, oral antibiotics for extensive involvement.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 40-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal papules distributed symmetrically on the flexor aspects of both wrists, with fine white lacy lines visible on close inspection, and similar white streaks noted on oral buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Psoriasis shows silvery scaling on extensor surfaces with Auspitz sign, not this morphology
Pityriasis rosea shows a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree trunk pattern, not flexor papules
Lichen simplex chronicus lacks this classic morphology or oral involvement
Correct - the 6 P's and Wickham striae with oral involvement define lichen planus
exp: Lichen planus is classically remembered by the 6 P's - pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules/plaques - with a predilection for flexor wrists, and Wickham striae (fine white lace-like lines) is a specific diagnostic clue, often accompanied by oral mucosal involvement which should prompt examination of the mouth in any suspected case.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 16-year-old boy presents with multiple open and closed comedones, inflammatory papules, and a few pustules over the forehead, cheeks, and chin, with onset coinciding with puberty and no scarring yet. Which sequence best describes the pathogenesis underlying his acne?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of the sebaceous gland by circulating antibodies
Androgen-driven sebum excess, follicular hyperkeratinization, and C. acnes-driven inflammation
Allergic contact dermatitis to a cosmetic product
Malassezia yeast proliferation within occluded hair follicles
why: Acne is not an autoimmune process targeting sebaceous glands
Correct - the four-factor pathogenic cascade of acne vulgaris
Contact dermatitis presents as eczematous change at contact sites, a distinct entity
Malassezia folliculitis presents as monomorphic itchy pustules typically on the trunk, without comedones
exp: Acne vulgaris pathogenesis is a four-factor cascade - androgen-driven sebaceous hyperplasia and sebum overproduction, follicular hyperkeratinization causing comedone formation, Cutibacterium acnes proliferation in the plugged follicle, and the resulting inflammatory cascade - understanding this sequence explains why treatment is layered by mechanism.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 22-year-old presents with multiple hypopigmented, finely scaling macules over the upper back and chest that become more noticeable after tanning; a KOH mount of skin scrapings shows short hyphae admixed with clusters of spores. What is the diagnosis?
why: Vitiligo shows completely depigmented macules with no fungal elements on KOH
Pityriasis alba shows fine hypopigmented facial patches in children and is KOH-negative
Tinea corporis shows an annular active scaly border, with septate hyphae but no spore clusters
Correct — classic tinea versicolor with pathognomonic KOH finding
exp: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur, part of normal skin flora; it produces hypo/hyperpigmented finely scaling macules, more visible after sun exposure since affected skin fails to tan, and is confirmed by the spaghetti-and-meatballs KOH appearance (short hyphae plus clustered spores).

subject: Dermatology
q: A patient presents with intense nocturnal itching and fine, linear, thread-like burrows in the finger web spaces, flexor wrists, and genital area, with similar itching now reported by three family members. The most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment are:
opts: Pediculosis corporis - permethrin 1% lotion to affected hair-bearing areas
Tinea corporis - topical clotrimazole 1% twice daily for 4 weeks
Scabies - permethrin 5% cream, whole body below neck, overnight
Atopic dermatitis - topical corticosteroid with emollients
why: Pediculosis (lice) affects hair-bearing areas, not finger webs with burrows
Tinea corporis shows an annular scaly plaque with a raised border, not burrows or nocturnal itch in multiple contacts
Correct — classic scabies presentation and first-line treatment
Atopic dermatitis is chronic and non-contagious, inconsistent with this acute contagious household clustering
exp: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, burrowing into the epidermis to produce intensely pruritic (worse at night) linear burrows favouring finger webs, flexor wrists, axillae, and genital region; it spreads readily through close contact, so household contacts should be treated simultaneously with topical permethrin 5% applied whole-body overnight.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 28-year-old man started on carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia 10 days ago presents with fever, painful oral and genital mucosal erosions, conjunctival injection, and targetoid and flat atypical target lesions with epidermal detachment involving about 8 percent of his body surface area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: EM major involves mucosa but is usually infection-triggered (especially HSV), with typical target lesions and minimal/no epidermal detachment
TEN is defined by over 30 percent BSA detachment, more severe than described
Correct, SJS is under 10 percent BSA detachment with mucosal involvement at 2 or more sites, drug-induced
Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease of the elderly with tense bullae, no significant mucosal involvement
exp: SJS/TEN exist on a severity spectrum defined purely by percent BSA epidermal detachment: SJS under 10 percent, SJS-TEN overlap 10-30 percent, TEN over 30 percent - carbamazepine is a classic trigger, usually started 1-3 weeks before onset. HLA-B*1502 association is well described in Han Chinese/Southeast Asian populations; extrapolation to all Indian populations is debated.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful, recurrent, malodorous nodules and abscesses with sinus tracts in the axillae and groin over the past 2 years, with scarring between lesions. What is the diagnosis?
why: Wrong — furunculosis is recurrent but discrete staphylococcal follicular abscesses, not interconnected sinus tracts with scarring.
Wrong — acne conglobata affects the face and trunk with comedones and nodules, not primarily flexural apocrine sites.
Correct — recurrent painful nodules/abscesses/sinus tracts with scarring in apocrine-bearing flexural sites is classic hidradenitis suppurativa.
Wrong — Fox-Fordyce disease is pruritic apocrine duct occlusion papules, not abscesses or sinus tracts.
exp: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic inflammatory disease of apocrine gland-bearing skin (axillae, groin, perianal, inframammary) — follicular occlusion leads to painful nodules, abscesses, interconnecting sinus tracts, and scarring, staged by the Hurley system (I-III). Managed with weight loss, smoking cessation, topical/oral clindamycin, and biologics (adalimumab) for severe disease.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 28-year-old sexually active man presents with a generalised non-pruritic maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, moist wart-like plaques in the perianal region, and generalised lymphadenopathy, appearing six weeks after a painless genital ulcer that had healed spontaneously without treatment. Which stage of syphilis does this presentation represent?
why: Primary syphilis presents only with the chancre and regional nodes, not a disseminated rash.
Correct — palmoplantar rash, condylomata lata, and lymphadenopathy weeks after a healed chancre define secondary syphilis.
Latent syphilis is serologically reactive but clinically silent, with no active lesions.
Tertiary syphilis appears years later as gummas or cardiovascular or neurosyphilis, not this acute picture.
exp: Secondary syphilis develops 4 to 10 weeks after the primary chancre heals, reflecting haematogenous dissemination of Treponema pallidum. Hallmarks are a symmetric palmoplantar maculopapular rash, generalised lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata, distinct from HPV-driven condylomata acuminata. Untreated, this stage resolves into a latent phase and may progress to tertiary disease years later.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 24-year-old woman develops multiple tender, erythematous, non-ulcerating nodules over the anterior aspect of both shins, two weeks after an episode of streptococcal pharyngitis, accompanied by low-grade fever and arthralgia of the knees. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — tender non-ulcerating shin nodules after streptococcal infection is classic erythema nodosum
Erythema multiforme produces target lesions typically on the extremities and palms, not tender nodules confined to the shins
Pyoderma gangrenosum causes ulcerating lesions with a violaceous undermined border, not simple tender nodules
Nodular vasculitis (erythema induratum) classically affects the calves and is TB-associated but tends to ulcerate, unlike erythema nodosum
exp: Erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis representing a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to an antigenic trigger — commonest being streptococcal infection, also tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, oral contraceptives, and inflammatory bowel disease — presenting as tender pretibial nodules that never ulcerate and resolve spontaneously over weeks, often with a bruise-like colour change.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 17-year-old girl with severe nodulocystic acne unresponsive to topical retinoids and oral antibiotics is being started on oral isotretinoin. Which counselling point is mandatory before initiating therapy?
opts: Isotretinoin is safe throughout pregnancy and needs no contraceptive precautions
Two reliable forms of contraception must be ensured for one month before, during, and one month after therapy
Sun exposure should be maximized to enhance drug efficacy
Isotretinoin has no effect on lipid profile or liver enzymes so no monitoring is needed
why: Wrong — isotretinoin is a potent teratogen, pregnancy category X.
Correct — dual contraception is mandated for one month before, during, and one month after therapy.
Wrong — isotretinoin causes photosensitivity, sun exposure should be minimized.
Wrong — isotretinoin classically raises triglycerides and transaminases, needing baseline and periodic monitoring.
exp: Oral isotretinoin is pregnancy category X, teratogenic, causing craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations. Two reliable contraceptive methods are mandatory for one month before, throughout, and one month after therapy, alongside baseline and periodic lipid profile/LFT monitoring for the drug's dyslipidemia and hepatotoxicity.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 22-year-old man develops multiple symmetric target-shaped lesions with three concentric zones over the palms, soles, and extensor forearms, one week after an episode of oral herpes labialis. Mucosal involvement is minimal and he remains systemically well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - HSV-triggered target lesions with minimal mucosal disease and preserved systemic wellbeing is classic erythema multiforme
SJS is typically drug-induced with prominent mucosal erosions and less than 10% BSA epidermal detachment
TEN is drug-induced with more than 30% BSA detachment, Nikolsky-positive, and life-threatening
Fixed drug eruption recurs at the same site on re-exposure to the culprit drug as solitary or few dusky plaques, not classic target lesions on palms and soles
exp: Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction most commonly triggered by HSV infection (recurrent EM is virtually always HSV-associated), presenting with classic target/iris lesions on acral and extensor surfaces, minimal-to-no mucosal involvement, and a self-limited, non-toxic course - contrast with SJS/TEN, which are usually drug-triggered, involve two or more mucosal surfaces, and make the patient systemically unwell.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 26-year-old man has a painful genital ulcer with ragged, undermined edges and a friable base, plus unilateral tender, fluctuant inguinal lymphadenopathy (a bubo) that has started to suppurate. Gram stain of the ulcer exudate shows Gram-negative coccobacilli in a school of fish pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — painful ragged ulcer, suppurative bubo, and school-of-fish Gram stain are classic chancroid
Primary syphilis produces a single painless, indurated ulcer with a clean base, diagnosed by darkfield microscopy/serology, not this Gram stain
Genital herpes causes multiple small painful grouped vesicles/shallow ulcers, diagnosed by PCR/Tzanck smear, not a single ragged ulcer with a suppurative bubo
LGV causes a small painless transient ulcer followed by prominent painful lymphadenopathy (the groove sign) but is chlamydial, not this coccobacillary Gram stain finding
exp: Chancroid presents with one or more painful, ragged/undermined genital ulcers plus tender, suppurative unilateral inguinal buboes; Gram stain showing Gram-negative coccobacilli in a school-of-fish pattern is characteristic of Haemophilus ducreyi — contrast with the painless, indurated, clean-based chancre of primary syphilis.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 68-year-old man presents with multiple tense, fluid-filled bullae over the trunk and flexural areas that do not rupture easily; the oral mucosa is spared and Nikolsky sign is negative. Skin biopsy shows a subepidermal blister with an eosinophil-rich infiltrate. The most likely diagnosis is:
why: Pemphigus vulgaris causes flaccid bullae, common oral mucosal involvement, and a positive Nikolsky sign from an intraepidermal split - the opposite of this vignette.
Correct - tense bullae, oral sparing, negative Nikolsky, subepidermal split with eosinophils, classic bullous pemphigoid in an elderly patient.
Pemphigus foliaceus causes superficial, crusted, scaly lesions rather than intact tense bullae, with a superficial subcorneal split, not subepidermal.

Dermatitis herpetiformis presents as intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles over extensor surfaces in coeliac disease, with neutrophilic papillary-tip microabscesses and granular IgA deposits - a different clinical and histological picture.
exp: Bullous pemphigoid, an autoimmune blistering disease of the elderly from autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins BP180/BP230, produces tense, intact bullae (subepidermal split) with oral sparing and a negative Nikolsky sign - the mirror image of pemphigus vulgaris, whose intraepidermal suprabasal split gives flaccid bullae, frequent oral involvement, and a positive Nikolsky sign.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 28-year-old obese woman presents with recurrent, painful, malodorous nodules and abscesses in the axillae and groin over the past 2 years, with sinus tract formation and scarring - a picture consistent with hidradenitis suppurativa. The primary pathological process in this condition originates in which structure?
why: Eccrine sweat glands are not primarily involved; hidradenitis suppurativa spares eccrine-gland-only areas such as the palms and soles.
Meibomian glands are sebaceous glands of the eyelid and are unrelated to hidradenitis suppurativa.
Correct - the disease begins with keratin plugging and rupture of the terminal hair follicle in apocrine-gland-bearing skin, triggering secondary inflammation.
Sebaceous glands are involved secondarily, but the primary event is follicular occlusion, not isolated sebaceous gland pathology.
exp: Hidradenitis suppurativa is now understood as a disease of follicular occlusion - keratin plugging of the terminal hair follicle in apocrine-gland-bearing areas (axillae, groin, perianal, inframammary) leads to follicular rupture, secondary inflammation, and abscess or sinus tract formation, rather than a primary infection of the apocrine gland itself. Risk factors include obesity and smoking; management ranges from topical or systemic antibiotics to biologics (adalimumab) and surgery for advanced (Hurley stage III) disease.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 24-year-old man returns from a beach holiday in Goa, where he walked barefoot on wet sand near stray dogs. Two weeks later, he develops an intensely itchy, serpiginous, thread-like erythematous track that slowly advances a few millimetres each day across the sole of his foot. What is the most likely diagnosis and its causative organism?
opts: Cutaneous larva migrans due to Ancylostoma braziliense/caninum
Larva currens due to Strongyloides stercoralis
Tinea corporis due to Trichophyton rubrum
why: Scabies burrows are short, straight or wavy tracks typically in the finger webs and wrists, not a rapidly advancing serpiginous track on the sole.

Correct - barefoot exposure to sand contaminated with dog/cat faeces followed by a slowly-migrating itchy serpiginous track is cutaneous larva migrans from animal hookworm larvae wandering in the epidermis.
Larva currens (Strongyloides autoinfection) migrates much faster, at centimetres per hour, and is typically perianal or truncal, not linked to beach sand exposure.
Tinea corporis presents as an annular scaly plaque with central clearing, not a linear migrating track.
exp: Cutaneous larva migrans (creeping eruption) follows walking barefoot on sand or soil contaminated with dog or cat hookworm larvae (Ancylostoma braziliense, A. caninum) - larvae penetrate skin but, lacking human-specific collagenase, cannot cross the basement membrane, so they wander in the epidermis creating an intensely itchy, serpiginous track advancing a few mm to cm per day. Treatment is oral albendazole or ivermectin; topical thiabendazole is an alternative.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 24-year-old man presents with a well-defined, round patch of complete hair loss on the scalp that developed over 2 weeks, with no scaling, erythema, or scarring. On examination, short broken hairs tapering towards the scalp are seen at the periphery of the patch, resembling exclamation marks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Tinea capitis typically shows scaling, broken hairs of variable length, and sometimes kerion/erythema, not exclamation mark hairs
Trichotillomania shows irregular, angulated patches with hairs of varying length from repeated pulling, not a smooth round patch with exclamation hairs
Correct
Androgenetic alopecia is gradual, patterned thinning (frontotemporal/vertex in men), not an abrupt well-defined patch
exp: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune, non-scarring hair loss presenting as sharply demarcated round or oval patches with a smooth scalp surface (no scaling or erythema). Exclamation mark hairs — short hairs that taper and narrow towards the proximal (scalp) end — are pathognomonic, resulting from abrupt disruption of the hair matrix by peribulbar lymphocytic infiltration.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 32-year-old man started on phenytoin two weeks ago develops fever, painful oral mucosal erosions, and target-like lesions with epidermal detachment involving 18% of his body surface area. Which diagnosis best fits this extent of skin involvement?
exp: The SJS-TEN spectrum is classified by percentage of epidermal detachment: SJS <10%, SJS-TEN overlap 10-30%, TEN >30%. This distinction drives prognostication (SCORTEN) and the threshold for burns-unit-level care; drug causality here is phenytoin, a classic offender.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 22-year-old woman presents with facial and body hirsutism that has developed gradually over 4 years since menarche, along with irregular menstrual cycles and mild acne, but no voice deepening, clitoromegaly, or increased muscle mass. What does the absence of these additional features suggest about the likely underlying cause?
opts: Confirms congenital adrenal hyperplasia as the cause
Indicates that idiopathic hirsutism with normal androgen levels is impossible
Favors a non-tumorous androgen excess state such as PCOS over an androgen-secreting tumor
exp: Gradual-onset hirsutism beginning around menarche, without rapidly progressive virilizing features (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, temporal balding, increased muscle mass), points toward a chronic non-tumorous hyperandrogenic state like PCOS; rapid onset plus virilization is the red flag that should prompt workup for an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumor.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid bullae over the oral mucosa and trunk that rupture easily, leaving painful erosions. Image described: gentle lateral pressure applied to normal-looking perilesional skin produces a new erosion within seconds. Which sign is being demonstrated, and it is characteristic of which level of skin cleavage?
why: Correct: Nikolsky sign reflects intraepidermal suprabasal acantholysis, as in pemphigus vulgaris
Asboe-Hansen sign is spread of an intact bulla by pressure on its top, and it too marks intraepidermal disease
Darier sign is urtication on stroking a mastocytosis lesion
Koebner phenomenon is new lesions at trauma sites, as in psoriasis or lichen planus
exp: A positive Nikolsky sign — shearing of clinically normal skin with lateral pressure — reflects loss of keratinocyte cohesion; in pemphigus vulgaris this cleavage is intraepidermal/suprabasal due to anti-desmoglein-3 antibodies, distinguishing it from the subepidermal split of bullous pemphigoid (Nikolsky-negative).

subject: Dermatology
q: A 24-year-old man presents with a single, painless, indurated genital ulcer with a clean base, present for 10 days, along with non-tender bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. He reports unprotected intercourse 3 weeks ago. Which test on ulcer exudate would most rapidly confirm the diagnosis?
opts: Tzanck smear for multinucleated giant cells
why: Correct — dark-field microscopy directly visualizes spirochetes before serology turns reactive.
Gram stain for gram-negative coccobacilli (school-of-fish pattern) is used for chancroid (H. ducreyi), which causes a painful ulcer, not this painless one.
Tzanck smear detects herpetic multinucleated giant cells, not applicable to a painless indurated ulcer.
KOH mount is for fungal infections, irrelevant to this presentation.
exp: Primary syphilis presents as a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy, appearing about 3 weeks after exposure. Dark-field microscopy of ulcer exudate is the fastest confirmatory test, since serology (VDRL/TPHA) may still be non-reactive this early in infection.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 30-year-old farmer presents with an itchy, annular, erythematous plaque on the forearm with a raised, scaly, advancing border and central clearing, present for 3 weeks. It has slowly enlarged despite an over-the-counter steroid cream. What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: KOH mount showing septate branching hyphae
Gram stain of the border scale
why: Tzanck smear detects viral multinucleate giant cells (herpes/varicella), not dermatophytes.
Dark-field microscopy is for spirochetes (syphilis), irrelevant here.
Correct — KOH mount of the active border shows septate branching hyphae, confirming dermatophytosis.
Gram stain identifies bacteria, not fungal elements, and this presentation is classic dermatophytosis, not a bacterial infection.
exp: Tinea corporis presents as an annular plaque with a scaly, actively advancing border and central clearing; topical steroids paradoxically worsen and disguise it (tinea incognito). KOH mount of scale from the active edge showing septate branching hyphae is the bedside confirmatory test before starting an oral or topical antifungal.

subject: Dermatology
q: A 6-week-old infant presents with greasy yellow scales over the scalp vertex (cradle cap) along with mild erythema in the nasolabial folds and diaper area. The infant is otherwise thriving with normal feeding and growth. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Gentle emollients/mineral oil with soft-brush scale removal and reassurance
Referral for skin biopsy to exclude Langerhans cell histiocytosis
why: Correct — conservative emollient care with reassurance is sufficient for this self-limiting, thriving-infant presentation.
Systemic antifungals are unnecessary for a mild condition confined to sebaceous areas.
High-potency topical steroids are unnecessary and risky on infant skin for a self-resolving condition.
Biopsy/LCH workup is reserved for atypical, ulcerating, or systemic-symptom presentations, not typical thriving-infant cradle cap.
exp: Infantile seborrheic dermatitis (cradle cap) is a benign, self-limiting condition related to maternal androgen-stimulated sebum and Malassezia colonization in sebaceous-gland-rich areas; gentle emollients and scale removal suffice, with resolution by 6-12 months. Distinguishing it from atopic dermatitis (itchy, extensor/flexural, older infants) is a common exam discriminator.

subject: Dermatology
q: A newborn has generalized hypopigmentation of skin and hair, nystagmus, and photophobia. Fundus exam shows a translucent iris and absent foveal reflex. The parents are non-consanguineous but both have very fair skin. Which enzyme defect most commonly underlies this presentation?
why: Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes alkaptonuria (dark urine, ochronosis), not hypopigmentation.
Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes phenylketonuria, which can mildly hypopigment skin/hair but does not classically produce this ocular triad.
HMG-CoA reductase is a cholesterol-synthesis enzyme, unrelated to pigmentation.
Correct — tyrosinase deficiency impairs melanin synthesis, producing the classic skin, hair and ocular findings of oculocutaneous albinism.
exp: Oculocutaneous albinism results from defective melanin synthesis, classically due to tyrosinase deficiency (OCA1); the ocular findings — nystagmus, iris transillumination, foveal hypoplasia — occur because melanin is required for normal optic pathway and foveal development, not just skin colour. This distinguishes it from vitiligo (autoimmune melanocyte destruction, normal eyes).

subject: Dermatology
q: A 14-month-old child has multiple reddish-brown macules and plaques over the trunk. When one lesion is firmly stroked, it becomes raised, red, and itchy within minutes. The mother reports similar swelling after the child's last vaccine injection site was rubbed. Which of the following best explains this finding?
opts: Auspitz sign due to thinned suprapapillary epidermis
Koebner phenomenon at sites of trauma
Darier's sign from mast-cell degranulation and histamine release
why: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on scale removal) is specific to psoriasis, not this pigmented lesion.
Koebner phenomenon describes new lesions forming at trauma sites over days, not an immediate wheal on stroking.
Correct — Darier's sign indicates mast-cell degranulation, diagnostic of cutaneous mastocytosis.
Nikolsky sign is skin sliding off with lateral pressure from intraepidermal/subepidermal cleavage (pemphigus/TEN), unrelated to this reaction.
exp: Darier's sign — a pigmented lesion becoming a wheal with erythema and itch when stroked — reflects mast-cell degranulation and histamine release, diagnostic of cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa) in a young child. It is a distinct bedside sign from Auspitz (psoriasis), Koebner (psoriasis/lichen planus/vitiligo), and Nikolsky (pemphigus/TEN) — a common sign-matching exam trap.
